chapter: Wax Records, Broadway shows and Eddie Condon
title: Founding Wax Records
summary: Nicky Peters funds the label; Hall describes the artists, tunes like Am I Blue and good reviews.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: All right, so, we are in the midst of the fourties and, when did you start your record company, say '46?
'46, yeah.
And when did you start getting into the Broadway show thing?
Kind of simultaneous?
Yeah.
How did Wax Records come about?
Nicky Peters, a very beautiful lady, maybe I don't want to put this on record.
Well, then, tell it the way you want to tell it.

Her father gave her $1500 for a birthday present and this is circa 52nd Street, and she says, my dad gave me $1500 for a birthday present and I want to start a record company and I want you to handle it but I don't want to be known as the sponsor of that, and that's how it came about. So, I got Ben Webster and Jimmy Jones; am I leaving out somebody? Dick Vance. Well, originally it was Bill Coleman but he had already gone to Paris. He did return on a visit and made a

Wax record. But I wasn't the bass player on that, John Levy, was because when we made our first Wax Record, and we got mention for three out of four sides, this was the borderline between swing and bop. This was the last of that sort of thing and Mike Levine gave me a nice writeup in Downbeat.
Oh, yeah, your records were very well received. They were beautiful records. 'Emmaline', -- 'Am I Blue.'
Yeah, and we searched these titles, these tunes. The day we recorded -- 'Am I Blue' hadn't been recorded in 20 years, with Ethel Waters, and the day we recorded, Bing Crosby came out with it.
You mean the day it was released the day you record?
Yeah. But 'Emmaline' hadn't been --
No.

And 'Blues In My Heart' had always been a favorite of mine when I first started playing bass, Benny Carter, God bless him and when Ellis Larkins and I worked together, we used the same arrangement and the bass pattern that I got from Cliff Jackson, it went de-de-de-de- -- and I always used that.
Did you also do 'Bluebells of Harlem?' [ON WAX RECORDS]
Yeah, that was John Levy.
That was John Levy.
